title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Gave Back Searches and Paddlings
dek: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six cases gradually map out the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Court, while declaring that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves," also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, narrowing the boundaries of those rights.
why: Each case is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key rulings, ideal for listeners who want to grasp the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and backpack searches in American public schools in one go.
who: Parents, middle and high school teachers, law students, and anyone wanting to understand the boundary between government power and children's rights in American public schools.
skip: Listeners familiar with the Establishment Clause can skip the second case; if you know the details of the earlier cases, jump to the corporal punishment and search cases after 25:40.

points.h: Flag Salute Case: Student Rights Enter the School
points.body: Can students really claim First Amendment rights during class? The case actually started with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed saluting the flag violated the commandments against other gods and idolatry, so they refused to salute and pledge. In 1940, the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused to recite the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and parents could be fined or jailed. In 1943, the Court overturned the ruling 6-3. Justice Jackson wrote on Flag Day: no official can define orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other opinions; students need not utter words that contradict their hearts or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students have some First Amendment rights on campus.

During the Cold War, America portrayed itself as a nation "under God," adding those words to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951, the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, non-denominational prayer, leaving adoption to local districts. Districts that used it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students still sued. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale ruled 6-1 that it was unconstitutional; the key was not coercion but that the prayer was written by the government, itself constituting an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same power that can establish Christianity to the exclusion of all other religions may establish with equal ease any particular sect of Christians. The decision sparked fierce backlash, with plaintiff families mocked and harassed.

In December 1965, Des Moines middle and high school students planned to wear black armbands to protest US involvement in Vietnam. The school announced in advance that refusal to remove them would lead to suspension, yet some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 for the students. The issue was not ordinary dress code but a quiet, passive expression akin to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Without evidence of actual or materially substantial interference with schoolwork, schools may not suppress student opinion. The opinion stated: public schools are not totalitarian enclaves; students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This "substantial disruption" standard became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would resist nearly all rules; the hosts noted this slippery slope argument sounds quite absurd.

In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper The Spectrum had two articles that made principal Reynolds uneasy: one on teen pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled 5-3 for the school. The key distinction was between "tolerating student speech" and "promoting student speech": the paper was funded by the school, readers would assume school endorsement, and the articles were indeed immature in journalistic ethics. The Court held that schools may regulate content they promote. This drew the first clear boundary around Tinker's rights.

points.h: Corporal Punishment Not Cruel and Unusual
points.body: Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was young, and research showed corporal punishment has not disappeared in the US. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's regulation paddle was less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with one to five strokes per incident; but Ingram received more than 20 strokes in a single event and needed medical attention. The Court did not dwell on whether this particular case was excessive but ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reason: the Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons; prisoners and schoolchildren are separated by the "harsh facts of criminal conviction and incarceration." Schools are open places with teachers and peers as witnesses, and students go home after school. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states, actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students, and disabled students paddled at significantly higher rates.

points.h: Backpack Search Needs Only Reasonable Suspicion
points.body: In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the bathroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued searching and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and sentenced to one year of probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the search was legal. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have an expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause required for police; they only need the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

terms.def: The threshold established in Tinker for disciplining student speech: actual material disruption or evidence that it would substantially interfere with schoolwork.
The First Amendment clause prohibiting the government from establishing or endorsing religion, originally applying only to the federal government but extended to states via the Fourteenth Amendment.
A lower evidentiary standard than probable cause, applied to school officials' searches of student belongings.
The higher evidentiary standard required for police arrests or searches, contrasted here with reasonable suspicion for in-school searches.
Punishment involving physical pain, in this episode referring to paddling students' buttocks with a wooden board.
People who can only passively receive what the state chooses to indoctrinate, unable to express their own opinions.

It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate. This has been the unmistakable holding of this court for almost 50 years.

In our system, state-operated schools may not be enclaves of totalitarianism. School officials do not possess absolute authority over their students. Students in school as well as out of school are persons under our Constitution. They are possessed of fundamental rights which the state must respect, just as they themselves must respect their obligations to the state.
